what_it_does: Sparse matrix multiplication (multiplying two matrices where most entries are zero, so you only store and compute the non-zero values) is a fundamental operation in both AI and scientific computing, but its irregular memory-access patterns make it hard to accelerate efficiently on hardware. This paper presents VSpGEMM, an accelerator built on an AMD Xilinx Versal chip — a device that combines traditional programmable logic (like an FPGA, which lets you define custom circuits) with specialized AI Engine (AIE) processor tiles (small, fixed-function math processors arranged in a grid on the same chip). The key contribution is a new way of storing sparse matrices called BCSX (Block-wise Compressed Storage) that organizes non-zero values into fixed-size blocks, turning the normally unpredictable memory accesses into regular, predictable patterns that hardware can handle efficiently. A multi-level tiling strategy (breaking the computation into a hierarchy of chunks that fit into successively smaller, faster memory levels) and a carefully designed split between the AIE tiles and the programmable logic together reduce the overhead of merging partial results and transferring data between parts of the chip.
